title: Approaching Thunder Storm
description: Painted in 1859 by Martin Johnson Heade, this masterwork captures the eerie stillness of a Rhode Island salt marsh just before a thunderstorm breaks. The sky presses low and bruised above a luminous wedge of light along the horizon, casting the marshland grass and still water in an unearthly golden glow. Heade's flawless tension between calm and approaching violence made this one of the defining paintings of American Luminism.

title: Dish with flowers and birds
description: This exquisite hard-paste porcelain dish was produced in Jingdezhen, China, around 1700 for the European export market. Decorated with cobalt-blue flowering branches and perching birds, it exemplifies the Qing dynasty's mastery of export ware. The delicate imagery and precise, jewel-like glaze reflect the centuries of ceramic tradition that made Chinese porcelain the most prized luxury object in 18th-century Europe.

title: American Barque "Jane Tudor," Conway Bay
medium: Salted paper print from glass negative
description: Taken around 1855 by David Johnson, this salted paper print from a glass negative documents the American merchant barque Jane Tudor riding at anchor in the calm waters of Conway Bay, Wales. The photograph's extraordinary tonal range captures the ship's rigging against an overcast sky with documentary precision, offering a rare visual record of mid-19th century maritime trade and the golden age of sail.

title: Head of a ruler
description: This commanding copper-alloy portrait head, cast around 2300-2000 BCE, is believed to represent an Akkadian ruler of ancient Mesopotamia. The sharply defined brows, almond-shaped eyes, and carefully braided beard convey authority and divine status. One of the earliest known large-scale metal portraits in human history, this work predates most Western portrait tradition by two millennia and stands as a supreme embodiment of Akkadian royal imagery.

title: Christ Crowned with Thorns
artist: Antonello da Messina (Antonello di Giovanni d'Antonio)
medium: Oil, possibly over tempera, on wood
description: Painted around 1470 by the Sicilian master Antonello da Messina, this small devotional panel shows Christ at the moment of his crowning with thorns. Antonello's mastery of Flemish oil technique — absorbed during his time in Naples — gives the skin, thorns, and cloth a jewel-like precision. Christ's direct, sorrowful gaze invites the viewer into profound empathy, making this one of the most moving devotional images of the Italian Renaissance.

title: The Crucifixion with the Virgin and Saint John
description: Completed around 1624-25 by Hendrick ter Brugghen, the leading Dutch Caravaggist of his generation, this large canvas places the viewer in close intimate proximity to the Crucifixion. The Virgin and Saint John flank the cross with grief rendered through extraordinary emotional honesty. Ter Brugghen's mastery of Caravaggesque chiaroscuro - dark backgrounds slashed by warm sculpting light - gives the scene an emotional urgency that borders on the unbearable.

title: The Birth of the Virgin
description: Painted in 1467 by Fra Carnevale, a Dominican friar trained in Florence and Urbino, this monumental panel is one of the most ambitious architectural compositions of the early Italian Renaissance. The interior of a grand palazzo opens onto layered rooms filled with elegantly dressed figures celebrating the Virgin's birth. Fra Carnevale's mastery of perspective and his synthesis of Florentine rationalism with courtly Urbino refinement make this a landmark of Renaissance painting.

title: The Meditation on the Passion
description: Painted around 1490 by Vittore Carpaccio, this profoundly meditative work shows a solitary saint — possibly Job or Jerome — seated on a stone in a landscape strewn with symbolic objects: animal skulls, ruins, a stone throne, and an owl perched on a branch. The meticulous detail and uncanny stillness create an atmosphere of deep contemplation on mortality and the transience of earthly life, set against the luminous blue of a Venetian sky.

title: The Coronation of the Virgin
description: Painted after 1595 by Annibale Carracci, the reformist Bolognese master who reinvented Italian painting after Mannerism, this luminous composition shows the Virgin Mary crowned in heaven by Christ amid a swirling company of angels. Carracci's blend of Raphael's classical harmony, Titian's colorism, and a new naturalistic directness was enormously influential, shaping a century of European religious painting from Rome to Paris.

title: The Martyrdom of Saint Barbara
description: Painted around 1510 by Lucas Cranach the Elder, court painter to the Electors of Saxony, this dramatic altarpiece panel depicts the final moments of Saint Barbara, patron of those in danger of sudden death. The saint receives her martyrdom with serene composure while her executioner raises his sword against a backdrop of twisted Germanic trees and distant spires — a quintessential example of Cranach's ability to fuse devotional intensity with Northern landscape painting.

title: Virgin and Child with Four Angels
description: Painted around 1510-15 by Gerard David, the last great master of the Bruges school, this intimate Marian panel shows the Christ Child nursing while four angel musicians play for the Virgin. David is celebrated for combining Flemish technical precision with a tender domesticity that feels both sacred and deeply human. The soft luminosity of his surfaces and his meticulous rendering of textiles and skin place him at the summit of late medieval Flemish art.

title: Madonna and Child
medium: Tempera, oil, and gold on wood
description: Painted around 1480 by Vincenzo Foppa, the founding father of Lombard Renaissance painting, this tempera and gold panel captures the Virgin in a tender embrace with the infant Christ. Foppa's style is characteristic of the Milanese school — slightly austere, with an interest in three-dimensional form and a palette of cool, silvery tones — representing a pivotal moment in the transition from the International Gothic to full Renaissance naturalism in northern Italy.

title: Saint Christopher and the Infant Christ
description: Created around 1473 by Domenico Ghirlandaio, the Florentine master who trained the young Michelangelo, this large-scale fresco depicts Saint Christopher — patron of travelers — wading a river with the Christ Child on his shoulders. Ghirlandaio's luminous landscape and assured draughtsmanship reflect the confidence of the mature Florentine Renaissance. The monumental figure fills the picture plane with a directness and warmth that made Saint Christopher frescoes ubiquitous on church doorways throughout Europe.

title: Josefa de Castilla Portugal y van Asbrock de Garcini (1775–about 1850)
description: Painted in 1804 by Francisco de Goya, court painter to the Spanish Crown, this magnificent society portrait depicts Josefa de Castilla Portugal y van Asbrock de Garcini, a noblewoman of the Spanish aristocracy. Goya renders her with penetrating psychological acuity — the quiet dignity of her expression and the luminous rendering of her silk dress and lace mantilla belie the upheaval beginning to tear apart the old European order. One of Goya's finest formal portraits of the period.

title: Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zuñiga (1784–1792)
description: Painted in 1787-88 by Francisco de Goya, this is perhaps the most beloved childhood portrait in the history of Western art. The boy Manuel Osorio, age three or four, stands in a brilliant red suit holding a string attached to a pet magpie, while three cats lurk in the shadows behind eyeing the bird with predatory intent - a detail that transforms this charming image into a quietly unsettling meditation on the fragility of childhood innocence.

title: The Adoration of the Shepherds
description: Painted around 1605-10 by El Greco, the Greek-born master who spent most of his career in Toledo, Spain, this late Adoration of the Shepherds is among his most mystical works. The composition is dominated by divine light radiating from the newborn Christ, illuminating the ecstatic elongated figures of the Virgin, Joseph, and the shepherds in an unearthly glow. El Greco's signature flickering brushwork and acid palette give the scene an almost visionary intensity unmatched in his era.

title: Portrait of an Old Man
description: Painted around 1595-1600 by El Greco, this is one of his most searingly honest portraits. The elderly man - likely a theologian or cleric from El Greco's Toledo circle - confronts the viewer with an unflinching directness. El Greco's swift expressive brushstrokes dissolve the boundary between flesh and spirit, giving the sitter a quality that seems simultaneously earthly and otherworldly. It is a portrait of a soul as much as of a face.

title: Tommaso di Folco Portinari (1428–1501); Maria Portinari (Maria Maddalena Baroncelli, born 1456)
description: Painted around 1470 by Hans Memling, the Flemish master based in Bruges, this diptych portrays the Florentine banker Tommaso Portinari — agent of the Medici in Bruges — and his young wife Maria Baroncelli, posed as donors against a sky of luminous blue. The extraordinary precision of Memling's technique, his mastery of light falling across silk and velvet, and his nuanced characterisation of each face make this among the finest examples of 15th-century Flemish portraiture.

title: Virgin and Child
description: Painted in the 1670s by Bartolome Esteban Murillo, the most celebrated religious painter of 17th-century Seville, this glowing canvas distills his art to its most essential form. The Virgin - an ordinary Sevillian woman, young and tender - nurses the infant Jesus while warm golden light suffuses the scene from above. Murillo's genius lay in making the sacred feel intimately human and the human feel touched by the divine, a quality that made his Madonnas beloved across the Catholic world.

title: The Penitence of Saint Jerome
description: Painted around 1515 by Joachim Patinir of Dinant, the first European painter to be identified by his contemporaries primarily as a landscape painter, this small triptych shows Saint Jerome in his desert hermitage set within an immersive panoramic landscape. The earth is rendered in Patinir's signature bird's-eye view, stretching to a misty blue horizon of jagged rocks, rivers, and distant towns. The human figure exists within nature rather than dominating it — a revolutionary rethinking of pictorial space.

title: Charity
description: Painted around 1630 by Guido Reni, the most celebrated Italian painter of his generation, this monumental allegory of Charity shows a beautiful woman suckling two infants while a third clings to her. Reni's refined, silvery palette, idealized forms, and softly diffused light elevate the composition into a vision of pure virtue and selfless love. The painting embodies the Bolognese Accademia's belief that beauty and moral elevation were inseparable — that to paint the ideal was to reveal the divine.

title: The Holy Family with the Young Saint John the Baptist
description: Painted around 1528 by Andrea del Sarto — called 'the faultless painter' by Vasari — this late tondo is one of the most refined devotional images of the Florentine High Renaissance. The figures of the Virgin, the infant Christ and Saint John the Baptist are arranged in a natural, pyramidal harmony, their expressions blending tender affection with a quiet gravity. Del Sarto's mastery of sfumato modeling, his chalky pastel palette, and the delicate misty landscape behind place this among his supreme achievements.

title: Madonna and Child
artist: Luca Signorelli (Luca d'Egidio di Luca di Ventura)
description: Painted around 1505-7 by Luca Signorelli, the Umbrian master whose use of muscular anatomically precise figures directly inspired Michelangelo, this circular tondo depicts the Virgin and Child against a gold ground. Signorelli's Virgin has a sculptural solidity and commanding physical presence unusual for the subject, and Vasari praised Signorelli as the key artistic bridge between ancient classical sculpture and Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling.

title: Interior of the Oude Kerk, Delft
description: Painted around 1650 by Emanuel de Witte, one of the great specialists in Dutch architectural painting, this canvas captures the cavernous Gothic interior of the Oude Kerk in Delft bathed in the cool, clear light of a northern morning. De Witte was the first Dutch painter to systematically explore the effects of light moving through stained-glass windows and whitewashed vaulting. The tiny figures scattered through the nave are dwarfed by the building, creating a profound sense of sacred space and human transience.

title: A Peasant Family
description: Painted around 1640-48 by Antoine Le Nain, one of three brothers who created the most remarkable body of French peasant genre painting of the 17th century, this small copper panel depicts a rural family in their home. What sets the Le Nains apart from contemporaries is the dignity they grant their subjects - these are not comic rustics but grave self-possessed individuals. The muted palette and sober stillness give the work an almost devotional weight.

title: Ia Orana Maria (Hail Mary)
description: Painted in 1891, the year Paul Gauguin first arrived in Tahiti in search of what he called a 'primitive' paradise untouched by European civilization, this large canvas reimagines the Annunciation in a Pacific island setting. A Tahitian angel approaches two women carrying fruit, while the Virgin stands to the side cradling a Christ Child rendered with Polynesian features. Gauguin's bold outlines, raw saturated color, and spiritual symbolism announce a radical break from Western tradition toward the primitivism that would shape 20th-century art.

title: Bowl
medium: Stonepaste; painted in blue and black under transparent glaze
description: This elegant 15th-century Islamic bowl was produced in the stonepaste tradition of the Near East and decorated in underglaze cobalt blue and black with intricate floral arabesques and calligraphic bands. The balance of the radial design, the depth of the cobalt blue, and the precision of the brushwork reflect centuries of accumulated skill in Islamic ceramic arts. Such bowls were luxury objects, associating their owners with a refined court aesthetic that valued beauty, order, and the word of God.

title: "Isfandiyar's Third Course: He Slays a Dragon", Folio 434v from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, silver, and gold on paper
description: This spectacular folio is from the Shahnameh (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp, the most ambitious illustrated manuscript ever produced at the Safavid court in Tabriz, painted around 1530 by a team of the greatest Persian miniaturists. The scene shows the mythic hero Isfandiyar in one of his seven labors — slaying a ferocious dragon in a landscape of writhing rock formations rendered in lapis lazuli, malachite, and gold. The painting's teeming energy and extraordinary precision represent the pinnacle of Persian book illustration.

title: Study of a Bird
medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on paper
description: Signed and dated 1634 by Riza-yi 'Abbasi, the most celebrated Persian draftsman of the early 17th century and the dominant figure of the Isfahan school under Shah 'Abbas II, this single-leaf study renders a bird with extraordinary sensitivity in ink and opaque watercolor on pale paper. 'Abbasi trained many of the finest Safavid miniaturists and was renowned for his fluid calligraphic line and for bringing a new intimacy and naturalism to Persian court painting. This small work distills his genius.

title: Great Indian Fruit Bat
medium: Pencil, ink, and opaque watercolor on paper
description: Painted around 1777-82 by the Mughal court artist Bhawani Das, working in Calcutta for the British naturalist Richard Johnson, this natural history study of a large Indian fruit bat fuses the Mughal miniature tradition with European scientific illustration. The bat is rendered with both documentary precision and aesthetic grace, its wingspan carefully recorded while its dark leathery texture is conveyed through delicate pencil and watercolor washes of impressive sensitivity.

title: Saint Anthony the Abbot in the Wilderness
description: Painted around 1435 by the anonymous Sienese painter known as the Osservanza Master — named for a celebrated altarpiece in the Basilica dell'Osservanza in Siena — this luminous small panel shows Saint Anthony the Abbot seated in a golden Sienese wilderness. The jewel-like tempera and tooled gold ground combine Gothic spirituality with a new, delicate Renaissance naturalism in the treatment of the landscape. Few Sienese panel paintings of this generation equal this one for quality and preservation.

title: Portrait of a Woman, Possibly a Nun of San Secondo; (verso) Scene in Grisaille
medium: Oil on wood; (verso: oil and gold on wood)
description: Painted around 1485-95, this tiny double-sided panel is the finest surviving work by Jacometto Veneziano, a Venetian miniaturist celebrated by contemporaries but unknown from any signed work. One side shows a young woman dressed as a nun of the convent of San Secondo in Venice, her identity still disputed; the companion side bears a white greyhound on a blue ground. The painting's miniaturistic scale and enamel-like finish reflect the influence of Flemish portraiture on Venetian art of the period.

title: Portrait of Alvise Contarini(?); (verso) A Tethered Roebuck
medium: Oil on wood; verso: oil and gold on wood
description: This companion piece to the nun portrait is also by Jacometto Veneziano and depicts Alvise Contarini, a Venetian nobleman, on its front face, while the verso is painted with a tethered roebuck on a blue ground. The two tiny panels were likely hinged together as a lover's diptych. Together they represent the most complete surviving example of Jacometto's work and offer an intimate window into Venetian aristocratic portraiture of the late 15th century.

title: Tabernacle House Altar with the Adoration of the Shepherds, the Adoration of the Magi, and the Annunciation.
medium: Ebony-veneered soft wood, silver gilt, rock crystal, agate, and reverse painted and gilded glass.
description: A remarkable object in two parts: the painted glass panels depicting the Adoration of the Shepherds, Adoration of the Magi, and the Annunciation in reverse-painted and gilded glass are from the second half of the 16th century. The elaborate ebony-veneered frame with silver-gilt mounts and rock crystal was added around 1865-90 by the Aachen goldsmith Reinhold Vasters, renowned both for extraordinary craftsmanship and for creating copies of Renaissance objects so convincingly period that museum curators were deceived for decades.

title: Self-portrait
medium: Tempera and gold leaf on parchment
description: Painted in 1558 by Simon Bening of Bruges, the last and greatest of the Flemish manuscript illuminators, this tiny self-portrait on vellum is the oldest known self-portrait by an illuminator in any medium. Bening depicts himself in old age, holding a miniature and meeting the viewer's gaze with quiet pride. At a time when oil painters on panel were the dominant artistic force, Bening's self-portrait asserts the dignity and intellectual ambition of the illuminator's art — a coda to a five-century tradition he brought to its final flowering.

title: Virgin and Child in Majesty
medium: Walnut with paint, tin relief on a lead white ground, and linen
description: Carved in walnut and originally fully painted and gilded around 1175-1200 in France, this rare Romanesque devotional statuette belongs to the type known as the Throne of Wisdom, in which the enthroned Virgin presents the Christ Child as the living embodiment of divine wisdom. Very few such sculptures survive in anything like their original condition; this example retains traces of polychrome ground and tin relief decoration, making it invaluable for understanding the use of color in Romanesque sculpture.

title: Martyrdom of Saint Lawrence
description: This vibrant panel of English Romanesque stained glass, created around 1180, depicts the martyrdom of Saint Lawrence on his iron gridiron. Among the earliest significant survivals of English medieval glass, it was likely made for a major ecclesiastical building in the north of England. The bold, jewel-toned pot-metal pieces and the expressive linear drawing — black vitreous paint on glowing color — represent medieval glass-making at its most confident, when windows were the primary medium for monumental sacred illustration.

title: Enthroned Virgin and Child
medium: Walnut with gesso, paint, tin leaf, traces of linen, and possible human remains
description: Carved in walnut with gesso, paint, and tin leaf around 1150-1200, likely in the Auvergne region of France, this seated Virgin and Child is a complete and largely intact example of the Romanesque Throne of Wisdom type. The rigidly frontal posture, the Christ Child's formal gesture of blessing, and the probable presence of sacred relics within the hollowed base made such sculptures the focal points of major pilgrimage churches throughout medieval France.

title: The Fieschi Morgan Staurotheke
medium: Gilded silver, gold, enamel worked in cloisonné, and niello
description: Made in Constantinople in the early 9th century, this exquisite Byzantine reliquary — a cross-box (staurotheke) — was designed to hold a relic of the True Cross and is one of the supreme achievements of Byzantine metalwork. Its exterior is covered in gold and gilded silver set with gold cloisonné enamel plaques depicting Christ, the Virgin, and saints in the formal hieratic style of the Macedonian Renaissance. The Fieschi Morgan Staurotheke is considered one of the finest portable devotional objects of the early medieval world to survive.

title: Bamboo in Snow
medium: Pair of hanging scrolls; ink on silk
description: Painted in 1774 by the Japanese Zen monk Dapeng Zhengkun, who came from China to Japan and became a significant figure in Obaku Zen, this pair of hanging scrolls depicts bamboo stalks weighted with heavy winter snow. The composition achieves its force through simplicity: bold sweeping ink brushwork and powerful negative space on silk convey both the physical reality of snow-laden bamboo and the Zen ideal of endurance through suppleness rather than rigidity.

title: Stela of the Steward Mentuwoser
description: Carved and painted around 1944 BCE during the reign of Senwosret I, second pharaoh of Egypt's 12th Dynasty, this limestone funerary stela commemorates the royal steward Mentuwoser, a senior official of the Middle Kingdom administration. The relief is organized in horizontal registers: Mentuwoser is shown seated before an offering table heaped with loaves, while vertical columns of hieroglyphs record his titles, epithets, and prayers for the afterlife. It is one of the Metropolitan Museum's most important Middle Kingdom objects.

title: Head from a Statue of King Amenhotep I
description: Carved in sandstone and originally painted around 1525-1504 BCE during the reign of Amenhotep I, second pharaoh of ancient Egypt's 18th Dynasty, this idealized portrait head once formed part of a colossal cult statue. The broad smooth forehead and serene almond eyes embody the New Kingdom ideal of royal divinity - simultaneously young, powerful, and eternally calm. Amenhotep I was later deified and worshipped as a patron saint of the artisans' village of Deir el-Medina.

title: Yuny and His Wife Renenutet
objectName: Statue, Yuny, Renenutet, pair, menat, music
description: Carved and painted around 1294-1279 BCE during the reign of Ramesses II, the greatest pharaoh of the New Kingdom, this dyad statue from Asyut depicts the royal scribe Yuny and his wife Renenutet seated side by side in formal eternal poses. Both figures wear linen garments and elaborate tripartite wigs, and their calm faces retain traces of original pigment that once made such sculptures brilliantly lifelike. The group was placed in Yuny's tomb to receive offerings for eternity.

title: Book of the Dead of the Priest of Horus, Imhotep (Imuthes)
objectName: Papyrus, funerary, Book of the Dead, Imouthes, Imhotep, Imuthes
description: This papyrus Book of the Dead, commissioned for the priest of Horus named Imhotep around 332-200 BCE during Egypt's Ptolemaic period, is one of the longest and most lavishly illustrated funerary manuscripts to survive from ancient Egypt. Its nearly forty feet of papyrus are covered with vivid vignettes of the deceased's journey through the underworld, the weighing of his heart against the feather of Ma'at, and his presentation to Osiris, in a style blending Pharaonic tradition with Hellenistic influence.

title: Portrait of a Woman
description: Painted around 1670 by Giovanni Battista Gaulli, known as Il Baciccio, the Genoese-born Roman painter best known for his breathtaking ceiling fresco in the Gesù church depicting the Triumph of the Name of Jesus, this confident portrait shows a young Roman noblewoman with a direct, assured gaze. The loosely rendered hair, softly luminous skin, and assured brushwork are characteristic of Gaulli's approach to portraiture — immediate, psychologically alive, and free from the stiffness of much 17th-century formal portraiture.

title: In proof of true love, a watercarrier skeleton arguing with a woman (Posada); two skeleton angels in upper corners (Manilla)
description: Engraved and printed around 1890-96 by Jose Guadalupe Posada, Mexico's most beloved and influential printmaker, this popular broadsheet depicts a skeleton watercarrier arguing with a living woman while skeleton figures witness the scene. Posada's calavera figures were produced in their thousands for Mexico City's mass-market press, at once comic, satirical, and deeply rooted in the Day of the Dead tradition in which death is confronted with laughter rather than dread. His imagery directly inspired the Mexican muralists.

title: Our Lady of Valvanera
description: Painted around 1770-80 in the Cuzco School tradition of colonial Peru, this devotional canvas depicts Our Lady of Valvanera - patron saint of La Rioja, Spain - enthroned in an elaborate gilded frame flanked by angels. The extraordinarily rich surface, heavy with applied gold, deep jewel-toned pigments, and intricate brocade patterns on the Virgin's mantle, is characteristic of the syncretic art tradition of viceregal Peru, where Andean craft sensibilities fused with European devotional painting.

title: Christ Carrying the Cross, called "The Lord of the Fall"
description: Painted around 1770-75 in the Cuzco School tradition of Peru, this intensely expressive image of Christ fallen beneath the weight of the cross belongs to the devotional painting tradition of the Viceroyalty of Peru. The use of oil and gold on canvas and the richly emotive face are hallmarks of the Cuzco School synthesis of Spanish devotional imagery with Andean artistic sensibility. Such works were central to popular piety in colonial Peru and remain objects of deep veneration today.

title: Portrait of Sor Juana de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe
description: Painted in 1797 in New Spain (present-day Mexico) by Domingo Ortiz, this formal portrait documents a nun of the Augustinian order identified as Sor Juana de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe. The sitter's composed dignity, the minutely detailed rendering of her religious habit, the black professed veil, the escutcheon of her convent, and the symbolic objects she carries are all carefully recorded according to the strict conventions of colonial Mexican nun portraiture. Such paintings were made at the moment of profession and served as family memorials.

title: Orchids and Rocks
description: Painted in 1888 by Yi Ha-eung, known to history as Heungseon Daewongun, the father of Korea's last king and one of the most powerful political figures of the late Joseon dynasty, this elegant hanging scroll depicts wild orchids and rocky ground in the ink-on-silk tradition of Korean literati painting. Orchids were the favored subject of Korean scholar-painters for centuries, symbolizing moral integrity, refined taste, and the ability to flourish far from worldly acclaim. Yi Ha-eung's brushwork is simultaneously controlled and spontaneous.
